Adding specifics from the lab runs we did against an open-source base model comparable to the one Atlas referenced. Notes below are from a controlled cluster (H100, 80GB) and assume fp16 quantization where applicable. These are synthetic-driver numbers (closed-loop with backpressure) to give an initial baseline — we will re-run against your anonymized prompts once received.

Methodology summary (brief):
- Driver types: open-loop (fixed QPS) for latency distributions; closed-loop (concurrency-driven) to identify saturation.
- Sequence lengths tested: 32, 256, 1024 tokens (prompt+completion).
- Concurrency sweep: 1–256 clients; step factor 2; 60s steady-state at each step.
- Metrics captured: p50/p90/p95/p99 latency, GPU util, memory, KV cache hit rate, tokens/sec.
- Artifacts: raw traces (jsonl), consolidated percentiles, perf counters, flamegraph snippets.

Key results (example baseline):
- 32 tokens (open-loop, target 400 QPS): p50 12ms, p95 34ms, p99 87ms.
- 256 tokens (open-loop, 120 QPS): p50 68ms, p95 180ms, p99 420ms.
- 1024 tokens (open-loop, 20 QPS): p50 420ms, p95 1080ms, p99 2200ms.

Scaling behavior observations:
- Linear throughput up to the GPU-bound region; latency p95 grows slowly until queuing/batching saturation is hit.
- In closed-loop saturation tests we observe a sharp p99 knee once GPU memory bandwidth is the bottleneck; recommended headroom is 30% below that knee for production SLOs.
- When concurrency doubles beyond headroom, graceful degradation modes kick in: 1) reduced batching windows (prioritize latency), 2) fall back to a smaller-quantized model variant, 3) region spillover to a lower-cost cluster.

Reproducibility and artifacts: we will share raw-run-0123.jsonl (traces) and a consolidated initial-results-summary.pdf for your audit team. Those include the test driver configuration, seed inputs, and deterministic random seeds used during the run.

Caveats: numbers above depend heavily on prompt distribution, temperature, and whether KV caching is effective across requests. We will re-run these with your anonymized payloads.

Tom — good questions, answers and next steps below. Quoting your points for clarity.

> 1) Full p50/p95/p99 traces for 256 tokens under 8/16/32 concurrent clients (raw timestamps).
We will provide raw-run-0123.jsonl that contains per-request timestamps, latencies, and the driver config. We'll also include a replay helper script and a README to map trace fields to your SRE's replay tool.

> 2) 24-hour soak: dedicated pool and SLA?
We can provision a dedicated H100 pool for the soak (Reserved pilot capacity). For pilots we provide a limited availability SLA (Uptime guarantee for the reserved window and incident response from our pilot support team). Noisy-neighbor effects are minimized by dedicated pools; for hosted pilots we use strict tenant isolation + quota enforcement and pro-active autoscaling policies. I'll include a short Rider doc that describes noisy-neighbor mitigation.

> 3) KV cache hit-rate and cross-client behavior.
KV caching is prefix-based: identical request prefixes benefit from shared KV entries if they hit the same model variant and routing shard. We'll provide example cache-hit histograms from the run. Note that cross-tenant sharing is never enabled — cache entries are scoped per-tenant.
